title: Asian Games Day 1: Xu Jiayu Sets Record at 31, Teen Stars Shine
summary:
At the 2026 Asian Games in Tokyo, day one of swimming brought a wave of record-breaking performances. The standout? Xu Jiayu of China, who won the men's 100m backstroke in 51.98 seconds — a new Games Record. At 31 years old, Xu is defying the typical peak age for swimmers. He has now won 13 consecutive Chinese national titles, starting when he was just 18, and owns five Olympic medals. His time easily cleared the previous Games Record of 52.23 he set three years ago.

The women's events were equally impressive. Yu Zidi of China, the youngest-ever swimmer to medal at the World Championships, kicked off her campaign with a dominant win in the 200m butterfly, clocking 2:05.08.

In the 50m breaststroke, Tang Qianting of China blasted a 29.45 to take gold, one of only two sub-30-second swims in the final. She erased her own Games Record of 29.50 set in the heats. Her time was just .05 outside the Asian Record of 29.44 she set earlier this year. Tang is a three-time Olympic medalist from Paris, with silver in the 100m breast and relay medals.

Joining her under 30 seconds was 35-year-old Satomi Suzuki of Japan, who touched in 29.91 for silver — her first-ever sub-30 swim and a new Japanese national record. The veteran's performance shows that experience can still challenge youth.

Finally, China's women's 4x100m freestyle relay team of Yu Yiting, Zhang Yufei, Cheng Yujie, and Wu Qingfeng combined for a Games Record 3:33.10. Yu opened in 53.39, Zhang blazed a 52.99, Cheng kept pace with 53.79, and Wu anchored in 52.93 to seal the gold. With world junior records, national records, and Games records falling, the stage is set for an exciting week at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre.
why_it_matters: Days like this show how elite sport balances youth and longevity, and they carry real consequences: Asian Games results help decide who qualifies for world championships and Olympics, and they influence the funding, coaching and public attention that national swimming programmes receive.

background_read: The Asian Games (a multi-sport competition for athletes from across Asia, run by the Olympic Council of Asia and first staged in New Delhi in the 1950s) are held every four years and work like a regional Olympics.

In swimming, medals are decided through heats — preliminary rounds — and finals, and only the fastest swimmers advance, which is why a swimmer like Tang Qianting can break a Games Record in the morning heats and then beat that same record again in the evening final.
The Tokyo Aquatics Centre, the venue named in this report, was built for the Tokyo Olympics, which were held in 2021 after the COVID-19 pandemic postponed them.

One quirk of the sport: the 50m breaststroke is not an Olympic event — the Olympics races only the 100m and 200m — so the Asian Games give sprint specialists such as Tang and Satomi Suzuki a rare stage of their own.

Xu Jiayu (a Chinese backstroke specialist and multiple Olympic medallist) is also swimming against a trend: swimmers usually peak in their early twenties, so a 31-year-old champion and a 35-year-old silver medallist stand out. China has long been one of the dominant swimming nations in Asia, and its relay squads often mix younger swimmers with Olympic champions such as Zhang Yufei.

perspectives.description: Asian swimming looks deeper than ever: a 31-year-old world-class backstroker, a teenage butterfly star and a record-breaking relay all on the same night. Veterans like Xu and Suzuki show that careers can stretch well past the usual peak, which is encouraging for athletes and coaches alike.

A Games Record is only a record within one region — it may still be far slower than the world record, and the fastest swimmers from other continents are not in the pool. Others worry about pressure on very young athletes like Yu Zidi, whose results are already being framed as records.

Swimming times have fallen steadily for decades because of better training, nutrition, video analysis and pool design, so records at a major meet are expected rather than shocking. The night also reflects a wider shift: Asian nations, especially China and Japan, now win medals across strokes that were once dominated elsewhere.

With the week only just beginning, the interesting questions are whether Tang can close the .05-second gap to her Asian Record and whether Xu and Suzuki can hold off younger rivals as the meet goes on. Results here also feed into the next Olympic cycle, shaping who competes at the following Summer Games in Los Angeles.
